cards.back: The market in which an issuer raises capital by selling new securities directly to investors, with proceeds going to the issuer. IPOs and additional offerings occur here.
An underwriting arrangement in which the syndicate purchases the entire issue from the issuer and resells it to the public, assuming the financial risk for any unsold shares.

Under Reg D, an individual with income over $200,000 ($300,000 joint) in each of the last two years or net worth exceeding $1 million (excluding primary residence), or certain institutions and credentialed persons (e.g., holders of Series 7, 65, or 82).
A broker-dealer that stands ready to buy and sell a specific security for its own account at publicly quoted bid and ask prices, providing liquidity to the secondary market.
When a broker-dealer acts as an intermediary executing a trade on behalf of a customer and charges a commission, rather than trading from its own inventory.

An order that becomes a market order once the stock trades at or through a specified stop price. Sell stops are placed below the market to protect long positions; buy stops are placed above the market to protect shorts.
The right of existing common shareholders to maintain their proportionate ownership by purchasing newly issued shares before they are offered to the public.
Preferred stock that accrues any skipped dividends; all unpaid (accumulated) dividends must be paid before any common dividend can be paid.

A negotiable certificate issued by a U.S. bank representing shares of a foreign corporation, allowing those shares to trade in U.S. markets in U.S. dollars. ADR holders face currency risk and generally lack voting rights.
The first day a stock trades without the previously declared dividend. Under T+1 settlement, the ex-date is the same business day as the record date for regular-way trades.
The total annualized return an investor earns by holding a bond to maturity, accounting for the coupon income, the time value of money, and any gain or loss between purchase price and par value.
A municipal bond backed by the full faith, credit, and taxing power of the issuer. GO bonds typically require voter approval and are repaid through tax revenues.
A municipal bond backed solely by revenues generated from a specific project or facility (e.g., toll roads, airports). Not backed by the issuer's taxing power.
A short-term money market instrument used to finance international trade, representing a time draft drawn on and guaranteed by a bank.
The per-share value of a mutual fund, calculated as (total assets − total liabilities) ÷ shares outstanding. Computed at least once per business day at market close (forward pricing).
A dollar level of mutual fund investment that qualifies the investor for a reduced front-end sales charge. Failing to inform a client of an available breakpoint is a prohibited "breakpoint sale."
An insurance contract whose separate-account value and payout fluctuate with the performance of underlying investments. Considered both an insurance product and a security; requires a prospectus.
A contract giving the holder the right (not the obligation) to buy 100 shares of the underlying security at the strike price before expiration. The writer is obligated to sell if exercised.

A municipal fund security offering tax-advantaged savings for qualified education expenses. Contributions grow tax-deferred and qualified withdrawals are federal tax-free; covered by a program disclosure document.
A limited partnership or similar entity that passes income, gains, losses, and tax benefits directly to investors. DPPs are generally illiquid, unlisted, and require suitability determinations.
An account in which the customer borrows from the broker-dealer to purchase securities. Reg T initial requirement is 50%; FINRA minimum equity is $2,000; maintenance is 25% long / 30% short.

A qualified retirement account allowing pre-tax (potentially deductible) contributions that grow tax-deferred. Withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income; RMDs begin at age 73; 10% penalty for withdrawals before 59½.

An account in which the registered representative may execute trades without the customer's prior approval for each transaction. Requires prior written customer authorization and prompt principal review of trades.
Risk that affects the entire market and cannot be eliminated through diversification. Includes market, interest rate, inflation (purchasing power), and currency risks.
SEC rule requiring broker-dealers to act in the best interest of retail customers when making recommendations. Four obligations: Disclosure, Care, Conflict of Interest, and Compliance.
A bond's annual coupon interest divided by its current market price. Measures the income return at the current price but ignores capital gain/loss at maturity.

IRS rule disallowing a capital loss when a substantially identical security is purchased within 30 days before or after the sale that generated the loss. The disallowed loss is added to the basis of the replacement security.

A dividend taxed at long-term capital gains rates (0%, 15%, or 20%) rather than ordinary income rates. Requires the underlying common stock to be held more than 60 days within the 121-day window around the ex-date.
A significant decline in economic activity, traditionally defined as two consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth. Falls within the contraction phase of the business cycle.
An economic theory advocating active government intervention through fiscal policy (taxation and spending) to stabilize the business cycle and manage aggregate demand.
The interest rate the Federal Reserve charges member banks for short-term loans from the Fed's discount window. Set directly by the Fed as a monetary policy tool.
The interest rate banks charge each other on overnight loans of reserves. Targeted (not set) by the FOMC through open market operations and the IORB rate.

The Securities Investor Protection Corporation, a nonprofit established by SIPA (1970) that protects customers of failed broker-dealers up to $500,000 per separate-capacity customer, including a maximum of $250,000 in cash.

The Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board, an SRO that writes rules for municipal securities dealers, brokers, and advisors. Does not enforce its rules; enforcement is by FINRA, the SEC, and banking regulators.
A FinCEN filing required for any cash transaction or aggregated same-day cash transactions exceeding $10,000. Must be filed within 15 days.

A confidential FinCEN filing required for transactions of $5,000 or more involving suspected money laundering, fraud, or other suspicious activity. Must be filed within 30 days of detection (60 if no suspect identified).

Buying or selling a security while in possession of material non-public information (MNPI), or tipping such information to others. Penalties under ITSFEA include criminal fines up to $5 million / 20 years and civil treble damages.

Under FINRA Rule 2210, any written (including electronic) communication distributed or made available to more than 25 retail investors within any 30-calendar-day period. Generally requires principal pre-approval.

The Uniform Application for Securities Industry Registration filed by member firms to register associated persons. Must be amended within 30 days of any reportable change (10 business days for statutory disqualification events).
Any business activity by a registered person outside the scope of his or her relationship with the member firm. Requires prior written notice to the firm before engaging in the activity.
